topics: Places of Worship: Church, Mosque, and Synagogue

data.title: Church, Mosque, and Synagogue
data.sourcePassage: A Christian church is designed to focus worshippers on God and the sacraments. Near the entrance stands the font, a basin used for baptism — the sacrament of entry into the Christian community. The nave is the main hall where the congregation sits. The altar, central to Catholic and Anglican worship, is where Holy Communion (the Eucharist) is celebrated, re-enacting Christ's Last Supper. The pulpit is where the sermon is preached; the lectern is where scripture is read. Many churches feature stained glass windows depicting biblical stories, helping worshippers to reflect on their faith. A mosque reflects Islam's core belief in tawhid — the absolute oneness of God. Because God cannot be depicted, mosques contain no images of humans or God. Instead, they are decorated with geometric patterns and calligraphy from the Qur'an. The mihrab is a niche in the wall indicating the direction of Mecca (qibla), towards which all Muslims face during prayer. The minbar is a raised platform from which the imam delivers the Friday sermon. Before entering the prayer hall, worshippers perform wudu — ritual washing — in the ablution area. The minaret is the tower from which the call to prayer (adhan) is traditionally announced. A synagogue is the Jewish centre for prayer, study, and community. The Aron HaKodesh (Holy Ark) is positioned on the wall facing Jerusalem and houses the Torah scrolls. Above it burns the Ner Tamid — the Eternal Light — symbolising God's continuous presence. The bimah is a raised platform from which the Torah is read aloud. In Orthodox synagogues, men and women sit separately; in Reform synagogues, they sit together.

topics: Places of Worship: Mandir and Gurdwara

data.title: Mandir and Gurdwara
data.sourcePassage: A mandir is a Hindu temple designed as the home of a deity. At its heart is the shrine room containing one or more murtis — sacred images or statues of Hindu deities such as Vishnu, Shiva, or Lakshmi. Hindus believe that the divine is truly present in the murti, so worship involves treating the deity like an honoured guest: bathing, dressing, and feeding the image. During puja, worshippers present offerings of flowers, water, and food. The aarti ceremony involves waving a lit lamp before the murti as an act of devotion. Prasad — food that has been blessed by being offered to the deity — is distributed to worshippers at the end of puja. Bells are rung to alert the deity to the worshipper's presence. Hindus may also worship at home shrines, making puja a daily personal practice. A gurdwara is a Sikh place of worship, meaning 'doorway to the Guru'. It is identified by the Nishan Sahib — a saffron-coloured flag bearing the Khanda symbol — flying outside. Inside, the most important feature is the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh holy scripture, which is treated as a living Guru. It rests on a raised platform called the takht and is covered with a decorative cloth (rumala) when not being read. Worshippers sit on the floor as a sign of equality — no one sits higher than the Guru Granth Sahib. Kirtan — the devotional singing of hymns — is central to worship. After the service, everyone is invited to eat together in the langar hall, where free food is prepared and served by volunteers as an act of sewa (selfless service). The langar is open to people of all faiths and backgrounds, expressing the Sikh values of equality and community.

topics: Places of Worship: Buddhist Temples and Comparing Worship

data.title: Buddhist Worship and Comparing Places of Worship
data.sourcePassage: Buddhist temples vary widely across traditions — Theravada temples in Southeast Asia look different from Zen temples in Japan or Tibetan monasteries — but share common features. Central to most is a shrine or altar containing an image of the Buddha. Importantly, the Buddha image is not worshipped as a god; Buddhism does not teach belief in a creator God. Instead, the image represents the qualities of an enlightened mind — wisdom and compassion — that Buddhists aspire to develop. Offerings of flowers, candles, and incense are placed at the shrine as acts of mindfulness and respect. Meditation spaces are a key feature of Buddhist worship, reflecting the central importance of mental training in the Buddhist path. Stupas — dome-shaped monuments originally built to house relics of the Buddha — are important features of Buddhist sacred sites. Worshippers walk clockwise around them as an act of veneration. Comparing places of worship across religions reveals both similarities and differences. All provide a space for community gathering and individual spiritual practice. Many feature a focal point for worship: the altar (church), mihrab (mosque), Aron HaKodesh (synagogue), murti (mandir), Guru Granth Sahib (gurdwara), or Buddha shrine (temple). Some contain no images — mosques and most Protestant churches — while others feature rich visual symbolism. All place importance on sacred texts, though where they are kept and how they are handled varies. Many also serve community functions beyond worship: the langar feeds anyone who comes, the church hall hosts community groups, and the synagogue provides Jewish education.
